title: Short Stature in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Short stature is height below the 3rd centile (‑2 SD) for age and sex. Identify growth pattern, distinguish normal variants from pathology, and target reversible causes common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Height < 3rd centile or > 2 SD below the mean for age/sex, confirmed on two separate measurements at least 3 months apart.
b: Plot on WHO growth chart; calculate height‑age Z‑score.
Assess growth velocity (cm/year) – < 4 cm/yr in a 2‑year‑old is abnormal.

sections.p: Stage severity by height‑age Z‑score and growth velocity.
b: Mild: –2 to –2.5 SD, normal velocity.
Moderate: –2.5 to –3 SD or velocity 4‑5 cm/yr.
Severe: < ‑3 SD or velocity < 4 cm/yr.

sections.p: Classify causes into constitutional, endocrine, chronic disease, genetic, and nutritional; in East Africa consider infections and socioeconomic factors early.
b: Constitutional (familial) short stature – normal velocity, parental heights low.
Chronic disease – HIV, TB, recurrent malaria, sickle cell disease, chronic kidney disease.
Endocrine – GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, pseudohypoparathyroidism.
Nutritional – protein‑energy malnutrition, micronutrient deficiency (zinc, vitamin D).
Genetic – achondroplasia, Turner syndrome, skeletal dysplasias, Rothmund‑Thomson syndrome.

sections.p: Parents notice child is markedly shorter than peers; may have proportionate or disproportionate limbs, delayed puberty, or associated dysmorphic features.
b: Proportionate: normal body ratios, suggests endocrine or chronic disease.
Disproportionate: short limbs, large head – suggests skeletal dysplasia.

sections.p: If radiography or hormone assays are unavailable, rely on clinical pattern, growth velocity, and basic labs; refer for specialist testing when possible.

t.a: Accurate height and weight measurement, WHO growth chart
t.b: Establish baseline and trend; confirms short stature and calculates velocity.
Helps differentiate familial from pathological short stature.

t.a: Basic labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, urine analysis
t.b: Screen for chronic infection, anemia, renal disease.
Detect hypothyroidism – high TSH, low free T4.
Low levels suggest GH deficiency; normal levels make GH deficiency less likely.
Delayed bone age supports endocrine or constitutional causes; advanced age suggests precocious puberty.
Positive test identifies HIV‑related growth failure; start ART.
Elevated PTH with low calcium points to pseudohypoparathyroidism.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent evaluation.
b: Severe growth deceleration (> 2 cm/yr loss).
Signs of chronic infection (fever, weight loss).
Cushingoid features, hypertension, hyperglycaemia.
Severe hypothyroidism (cold intolerance, lethargy).
Neurological deficits – suspect intracranial pathology.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause first; provide nutritional support and monitor growth.
b: HIV/TB/malaria – appropriate antimicrobial therapy, ART for HIV.
Hypothyroidism – levothyroxine (replace deficient hormone).
GH deficiency – recombinant GH (where available) after ruling out contraindications.
Nutritional rehab – high‑protein diet, zinc supplementation, vitamin D if deficient.
Genetic skeletal dysplasia – orthopaedic referral, avoid growth‑hormone therapy.

sections.p: Regular growth monitoring and early treatment of chronic disease improve final adult height.
b: Re‑measure height every 3‑6 months; plot on chart.
Address socioeconomic factors – food security, deworming, immunisations.
Educate caregivers on normal growth patterns and when to seek care.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic short stature but have different management.
b: Failure to thrive – primarily weight loss; height may be preserved.
Delayed puberty – height may be normal but growth spurt delayed.
Skeletal dysplasia – disproportionate limbs vs proportionate short stature.
Normal IGF‑1 does not exclude mild GH deficiency.
Bone age may be within normal limits in early endocrine disease.
Serum calcium can be normal in early pseudohypoparathyroidism.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid loss of height velocity, new onset hypertension, severe hypothyroid symptoms, unexplained fever or weight loss, signs of intracranial pressure.

faq.q: Is a child with low height always abnormal?
faq.a: No – if growth velocity is normal and parental heights are low, it is likely constitutional short stature.
Yes, when caused by treatable conditions such as infection, hypothyroidism, or nutritional deficiency.
It shows skeletal maturation; a delayed bone age suggests endocrine or constitutional causes, guiding treatment timing.

exam: What history points would make you suspect a chronic infection as the cause of short stature? — Recurrent fevers, weight loss, night sweats, known HIV or TB exposure, poor growth despite adequate nutrition.

A 7‑year‑old has height < 3rd centile, normal weight, and proportionate limbs. Thyroid tests are normal, IGF‑1 low. What is your next step? — Order a GH stimulation test; if deficient, consider GH therapy where available.

How does constitutional short stature differ from growth hormone deficiency on growth charts? — Both have low height, but constitutional shows normal velocity and parental heights within range; GH deficiency shows reduced velocity and low IGF‑1.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with short stature. Which investigations are essential? — CBC, reticulocyte count, renal function, serum ferritin, and bone age to assess chronic anemia impact.
Why is levothyroxine preferred over desiccated thyroid in hypothyroid short stature? — Levothyroxine provides consistent T4 dosing, avoids variable T3 levels, and has fewer side‑effects.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate referral for neurosurgical assessment? — New onset headaches, vomiting, papilledema, or focal neurological deficits suggesting intracranial mass.
Explain why growth hormone therapy is contraindicated in active malignancy. — GH can stimulate tumor growth; it is avoided until cancer is in remission.

In a low‑resource setting without IGF‑1 testing, how would you differentiate endocrine from nutritional short stature? — Look for signs of malnutrition (low weight‑for‑height), dietary history, and response to nutritional rehab; endocrine causes usually have normal weight and poor growth despite adequate intake.
